w: Dr. Abou-Arraj split this session in two. He recorded the first part (posted Nov 9): the periodontal phenotype, recession and how it is grafted, the lack of keratinized gingiva and the frenum. "The remaining two mucogingival deformities," gingival excess and abnormal color, he taught in the live class on Nov 12, after taking questions on the recording; his answers are folded into the sections they belong to. The class ended with his review for the final, which is in Exam Hints. The tissues: gingiva, alveolar mucosa and the MGJ The mucogingival junction (MGJ) separates the gingiva from the alveolar mucosa. You can often see it, but it is found "most accurately" clinically, with a probe. All the gingiva coronal to the MGJ is keratinized gingiva. Part of it is attached, to the root surface and the bone; the rest is free gingiva, the part a probe slips under to measure the probing depth. The line between free and attached gingiva isn't visible clinically. Mucogingival deformities Periodontal plastic therapy treats mucogingival deformities: "any deviation from the norm" in the volume, dimension, contour or shape of the soft tissue around teeth. The 2017 World Workshop classification (Journal of Periodontology, 2018) lists seven, and the slides walk through them in order: (1) the periodontal phenotype (thin scalloped, thick scalloped, thick flat); (2) gingival or soft tissue recession, described by surface (facial or lingual, interproximal or papillary), severity (Cairo RT1, 2, 3), gingival thickness and width, any NCCL or cervical caries, the patient's esthetic concern and hypersensitivity; (3) lack of keratinized gingiva; (4) decreased vestibular depth; (5) aberrant frenum or muscle position; (6) gingival excess (pseudopocket, inconsistent gingival margin, excessive gingival display, gingival enlargement); and (7) abnormal color (a mucogingival tattoo). The periodontal phenotype The phenotype has two parts: the tissue's thickness, thin or thick, and the gingival line's contour, scalloped or flat. Thin tissue can be judged by eye (you can almost see the roots through it), but the validated way is the probe: slide it into the sulcus. If you can see the probe through the tissue, the phenotype is thin, 1 mm or less. If you can't see it, the phenotype is thick, more than 1 mm. Why it matters: a thin phenotype is predisposed to recession, and recession that is already there tends to progress on it, while a thick phenotype resists it. His example: a young patient about to start orthodontics had a thin phenotype over his incisors, so thin you could see the roots. Orthodontic movement, then years of toothbrushing on top of it, would put him at risk of recession he didn't have yet. So before the orthodontics the phenotype was changed from thin to thick: a trapezoidal, full-thickness flap, a connective tissue graft from the palate sutured over the two central incisors (the teeth most at risk), and the flap put back over the graft to cover it completely. At two weeks the tissue was already thicker, and he was cleared for orthodontics with less risk of recession. Recession: what it is and who gets it Recession is "the location of the marginal periodontal tissues apical to the cemento-enamel junction" (AAP Glossary, 2001): part of the root is exposed. Measure it with the probe from the gingival margin to the CEJ, at the same six sites as probing depth, so it can be recorded and followed over time. It isn't only on the straight facial or lingual: note any interproximal recession too, because it "could change totally the prognosis of the treatment." It is common. The slide (Albandar and Kingman, 1999): 88% of people 65 and older and 50% of people 18 to 64 have at least one site with recession, and prevalence and extent rise significantly with age. In the recording he put it another way: more than half of the US population 30 or older has at least 1 mm of recession, and almost a quarter has at least one tooth surface with 3 mm or more. Older people have more not because of their age but because they have accumulated risk factors over more years. Recession is more common in men than in women and in African-Americans than in other groups, and most common on the buccal surfaces of maxillary molars (first molars in particular) and mandibular central incisors; canines are also commonly affected. Predisposing factors The slide lists ten: periodontal disease (periodontitis); trauma (toothbrushing, flossing, self-inflicted, foreign objects); anatomic variations (fenestration, dehiscence and abnormal tooth position); lack of keratinized gingiva; a thin gingival phenotype; orthodontic treatment; previous periodontal surgery; a high muscle attachment and aberrant frenum; iatrogenic factors related to the location of restoration margins; and the use of smokeless tobacco. What he added in the recording: Periodontitis, not gingivitis: attachment and bone loss expose the root. Previous periodontal surgery: after Phase I and resective Phase II therapy, "we caused most of this recession," on purpose, to leave an environment without pockets that the patient can keep clean. Toothbrushing is the most common traumatic factor: hard bristles, or an aggressive brusher whatever the bristle. The trauma list also takes in flossing habits, self-inflicted oral habits, foreign objects (a fingernail, a pen) and caustic medicaments applied directly to the gingiva. Anatomic variations. A fenestration is a window in the bone over the root; a dehiscence is missing facial bone from the crest apically. A tooth positioned buccally on the arch has thinner facial tissue and takes more of the toothbrush. Moving it back onto the arch orthodontically, into its alveolar housing, can resolve some of the recession, at least partly, without a graft. Put a dehiscence or fenestration together with a thin phenotype and an aggressive brusher, and you have "the perfect storm." Orthodontic treatment: pushing teeth buccally out of the alveolar housing (proclining incisors) over a thin phenotype can cause recession. Some studies find incisor proclination doesn't; he calls it controversial and advises caution about when to propose grafting. Iatrogenic margins: an intrasulcular or subgingival crown margin on a thin phenotype, an ill-fitting margin or an overcontoured restoration can lead to recession (which doesn't mean every crown needs a graft). A high frenum or muscle attachment pulls on the margin with every movement. Smokeless tobacco, held in one spot, usually the lower premolar or molar area, changes the tissue locally and can cause a severe localized recession. His worst case had no pockets and no interproximal bone loss, but recessions reaching the bottom of the vestibule, hard to treat even with several attempts. How recession develops Two mechanisms (from Zucchelli's textbook). Toothbrushing trauma, especially on thin tissue: the epithelium is abraded, the connective tissue under it responds with inflammation, an ulcer forms at the surface, and with continued trauma the margin recedes. Plaque-related: the same process as periodontitis (plaque in the sulcus with poor hygiene, apical and lateral migration of the junctional epithelium, loss of attachment), here on a local scale on a thin phenotype. "The key word here is inflammation": it is what actually causes recession, and the factors above are predisposing factors that make it happen. The Cairo classification: how much root can you cover? Before proposing a graft, assess how severe the recession is and what treatment can achieve. The Cairo classification (2011) reads it from the interproximal attachment. Attachment loss is the recession plus the probing depth, and interproximally it is measured mid-interproximal, not at the line angle; on anterior teeth the CEJ scallops up between the teeth. In health, with thin tissue, you probe about 1 mm mid-facial and about 2 mm interproximally. (For the exam he doesn't plan to give you a chart and ask for the numbers: "It's more general questions about recession types, one, two, and three.") The three types: RT1: recession with no loss of interproximal attachment; the interproximal CEJ can't be detected clinically on the mesial or the distal. The best prognosis: about 100% root coverage is achievable. RT2: recession with loss of interproximal attachment, where the interproximal CAL (from the interproximal CEJ to the depth of the interproximal sulcus or pocket) is less than or equal to the buccal CAL (from the buccal CEJ to the depth of the buccal sulcus or pocket). You can see the CEJ interproximally. Expect partial root coverage, about 50 to 60% in cases like his: at best up to the level of the interproximal attachment on either side. The tissue can't be pulled any higher, because there is no framework and no blood supply interproximally to hold it there ("if we know how to fix this, we could ... cure everybody from periodontitis"). His rule of thumb from the live class: on a tooth with more recession than its neighbors, the ceiling of what any graft can cover is the gingival margin of the adjacent teeth, the more apical of the two, whichever graft you use. RT3: loss of interproximal attachment where the interproximal CAL is greater than the buccal CAL. A graft for root coverage "would not end up achieving that root coverage at all," so root coverage isn't encouraged. The classification is how you decide when to propose a soft tissue graft for root coverage, and when not to. Why, as he explained it live: the root surface gives a graft no blood supply, so a graft and the flap advanced over it live on the bone and tissue on either side of the root (and apical to it). In RT3 that interproximal support sits too far apical. The surgery can be done, but "the outcome is not going to be that you gain any root coverage"; at most the tissue gets thicker. To cover those roots for sensitivity, esthetics or a high caries risk, the answer is more likely restorative. Why treat recession Exposed roots and lost tissue raise the likelihood of (1) dentinal hypersensitivity, (2) soft tissue discomfort (thin tissue with little keratinized gingiva can hurt to brush), (3) root surface caries, (4) esthetic concerns, (5) interference with adequate mechanical plaque control, and (6) greater susceptibility to inflammatory insult. And recession doesn't sit still: a systematic review (Chambrone and Tatakis, 2016) found that untreated recession defects continue to progress, the margin moving further apical. So "let's just monitor it" because it doesn't hurt, isn't sensitive and isn't in the esthetic zone doesn't mean it will stay the same. Apart from RT3, recession should be considered for treatment when indicated. (Restorative ways to treat recession are for next year's course; this session is about soft tissue grafting.) Soft tissue grafts: where they come from The two main sources in the US are the patient's own tissue, an autograft, and donor tissue from a tissue bank, an allograft; there are others (bovine, porcine). The most common graft comes from the palate (or the tuberosity), because the palate is orthokeratinized: its tissue "carries that information of keratinization with it" to the recipient site. Palatal connective tissue induces epithelial differentiation and keratinization. From the palate you take either a free gingival graft (FGG), the epithelium together with the lamina propria (the connective tissue) under it in one piece, or a subepithelial connective tissue graft (SCTG, or CTG), the connective tissue without the epithelium. The palate's layers, from the surface in: the epithelium (0.3-0.6 mm, thin), the lamina propria (connective tissue, 1.25-3.0 mm, usually the thickest), the submucosa (adipose and glandular tissue), then bone. An epithelialized graft is thin at 0.5-0.8 mm, average at 0.9-1.4 mm and thick at 1.5-2.0 mm or more. A thick graft brings much of the fat layer with it, and that is usually removed so it doesn't slow the healing. The anatomy to stay away from is the greater palatine artery and nerve, the neurovascular bundle. On the slide it runs about 7 mm from the CEJ in a shallow palate, 12 mm in an average palate and 17 mm in a high palate. So a high, deep palatal vault gives the most room for error when harvesting (the exam-review guide's point). There are guidelines for which area to harvest from (premolar, molar) and how far up the palate to go. In the live class: assess the depth of the palate from the start, because it sets how far apicocoronally the graft can extend; the shallower the palate, the narrower the graft. Within those limits you are more likely to hit a tributary of the artery than the artery itself, unless you reach the junction where the horizontal palate meets the vertical. Two ways to harvest a CTG: a trap door, elevating the epithelium and connective tissue together and then taking the connective tissue from under the epithelium; or harvesting the whole rectangle with its epithelium, like an FGG, and removing the epithelium afterwards. The exam-review guide puts it this way: sometimes an FGG is harvested but delivered as a CTG, because that is easier to harvest and heal. The rule for which graft: if the graft will be covered by a flap, it must be connective tissue only. The inner side of the flap is connective tissue, and epithelium placed against it "just would not heal properly." If the graft will be left exposed, not covered by the flap, use an FGG, with its epithelium. In the live class he framed it by the objective. For root coverage, the gold standard is a CTG under a coronally advanced flap; to increase the width of keratinized gingiva, an FGG. A CTG under the flap doesn't change the surface: a tooth with 2 mm of keratinized gingiva and 3 mm of recession still has about 2 mm of keratinized gingiva once it heals, but the root is covered and the tissue is thicker. An FGG left to heal on its own lets the palatal connective tissue induce keratinized epithelium. An FGG can cover some root too (his lower incisor case did several jobs at once: coverage for sensitivity, more keratinized gingiva, the frenum out of the way, a deeper vestibule), but on the same tooth a CTG with a coronally advanced flap gets more coverage. Root coverage with a CTG and a coronally advanced flap His case: recession on #10 and #11 (part of a composite filling was removed first). A trapezoidal flap, raised partial thickness to keep some of the periosteum, exposed the roots; the graft size was planned (a template helps) and a CTG harvested from the palate, its epithelium removed. The graft was placed and sutured, then the flap was advanced coronally over it, tension free, so it holds its coronal position covering the recessions and the graft completely. At about four weeks the coverage was good, and coverage that looks like this early usually holds. The profile view shows the other gain: much thicker tissue over the roots, a thick phenotype "that by definition would resist much better" further recession. "We always do a coronally advanced flap if we're trying to cover the graft." Many teeth: the acellular dermal matrix allograft Treating many teeth from the palate means a large, invasive harvest. When you can avoid that, use a soft tissue allograft: donated human dermis, usually from cadavers, processed to remove the epidermis, the hair follicles and the existing cells. What is left, the acellular dermal matrix (ADM, or ADMA; AlloDerm is one), is a matrix of collagen, elastic and reticular fibers with no cells. It wasn't designed for dentistry: it has been used since 1995 for burns, head and neck reconstruction, urology (bladder slings, pelvic floor reconstruction), orthopedics (rotator cuff repair, periosteal replacement) and hernia repair, and in dentistry since 1997, now in dental sizes. It is the most common soft tissue allograft (exam-review guide). Advantages (slide): it eliminates the need for a donor site; increases patient acceptance (no surgery on the roof of the mouth); decreases surgical time; treats multiple defects in one procedure ("quote-unquote unlimited quantities"); achieves esthetic results comparable or superior to autogenous tissue; and is easy to use. Disadvantages (recording): it is "more or less a dead piece of skin" with nothing to contribute to the healing, "like a band-aid." So it must be fully covered by the flap, because it heals poorly left exposed without a blood supply. Over time it is remodeled and replaced by the patient's own tissue (histology shows this). In a more demanding site it can't give the same benefit as autogenous tissue; the exam-review guide's summary is that allografts don't work as well as autografts but have many advantages. His case: canine to canine, five or six teeth, with a combination of RT2 and RT3 recessions. The flap was a tunnel (pouch): like an envelope flap but without raising the papillae, going into the sulcus of each tooth and connecting sulcus to sulcus into one plane under the tissue. The ADM went through two water baths, the second with tetracycline, was snaked into the tunnel over the roots, held with sling sutures, and the flap was advanced coronally to cover it completely. At six months, given the RT2 and RT3 start, the result was considered quite successful. Lack of keratinized gingiva Keratinized gingiva (KG) runs from the gingival margin to the MGJ, and it can be thin or thick. Besides the color change (pink gingiva, redder mucosa), find the MGJ by rolling the probe, held horizontally, from the mucosa toward the margin: the loose, mobile mucosa rolls with it, and at the MGJ the tissue stops rolling. From there to the gingival margin is the width of keratinized gingiva. It can be measured on edentulous ridges too. On average (Lindhe's figure), the maxillary facial KG is widest at the incisors, narrowest at the canine and first premolar, and wider again toward the molars, and the mandible follows a similar pattern; on the mandibular lingual it is narrowest at the incisors and widens toward the molars. Patients vary. Is keratinized gingiva needed? A zone of attached gingiva is, of and by itself, not essential for keeping periodontal health and attachment, when dental plaque is controlled and there are no other traumatic factors (Kennedy and colleagues, 1985; Scheyer and colleagues, the AAP Regeneration Workshop, 2015). If plaque control is suboptimal, at least 2 mm of KG is needed to prevent attachment loss. Many patients don't have optimal plaque control, so a tooth with less than 2 mm of KG is likely prone to recession. That doesn't mean every such tooth needs a graft: it is case by case. Not every patient lacking KG has recession, but lacking it predisposes to it, while a thick phenotype with a wide band of KG resists it. Gaining keratinized gingiva: an FGG left exposed His patient had an RT2 recession on a sensitive tooth with no KG: the site was a plaque trap, chronically irritating the margin and leading to more recession. The goal was to change the quality of the tissue, creating a band of KG; root coverage would be a bonus. A CTG under a coronally advanced flap wouldn't do it: covering the graft with the only tissue there, alveolar mucosa, gains no keratinized gingiva, because mucosa doesn't become keratinized just because it covers a graft. So he used a free gingival graft with an apically positioned flap: a trapezoidal flap (a horizontal incision and two vertical ones) placed apically, and an FGG from the palate, with its epithelium, left exposed so it heals into a band of KG, bringing its own determination to keratinize. Covering it with the flap would deny it that. The palate heals by secondary intention. The graft is held only by sutures, so patients are told not to pull the lip down to look at it every day, to keep a soft diet and not to brush the area while it heals. At three months there was a good band of KG where there had been none, blending with the neighboring tissue (bigger on the apical side), and partial root coverage, as expected for RT2. Her sensitivity was gone, the site was easier to clean and less of a plaque trap, and the phenotype was thicker and more protective. The frenum and the vestibule A highly attached frenum can be a critical factor in the progression of recession: with the lip and every muscle movement in the area (not only when someone pulls the lip), it pulls on the gingival margin, which facilitates plaque accumulation and adds to the recession. In one patient, pulling the lip pulled all the way to the margin of a central incisor with no KG. In another, the frenum stood in the way of the esthetic result while her crowns were being redone (the provisionals had closed the black triangle), so a frenectomy was done before the final restorations. It is a quick, easy procedure: dissect around the frenum, excise the tissue that forms it in a diamond shape, and close the diamond with a few sutures that extend into the lip. The classification lists decreased vestibular depth beside it, and the slides show both together. Gingival excess Gingival excess has four causes, each with its own treatment. The first is the pseudopocket, in gingivitis. Swollen, edematous gingiva on an incisor may probe 4 or 5 mm and bleed, but there is no attachment loss and no bone loss on the radiograph: the margin has moved coronally, the CEJ hasn't. Treatment: improved oral hygiene, and scaling where there is calculus. It is reversible and resolves. The second is gingival enlargement from medications, a gingival disease modified by medication, so plaque-induced gingivitis is always the primary factor. The three classes: anticonvulsants (phenytoin is the most documented), calcium channel blockers (common blood pressure drugs) and immunosuppressants (especially cyclosporine). The one you'll meet most in everyday practice is the calcium channel blocker. Oral hygiene and scaling come first (SRP only if there is periodontitis), but they won't resolve it: the tissue is fibrotic, with extra collagen fibers laid down in response to the drug, so it has to be resected surgically, a gingivectomy with a bur, a blade or a laser. Despite everyone's best efforts, you may need to ask the patient's physician or cardiologist whether they can switch the medication. The third is inconsistent gingival margins, a gingival line discrepancy between contralateral teeth (#8 and #9 not symmetrical, or margins stepping all over the place). It isn't pathologic, but no patient would be happy with how it looks, and it is more common than drug-induced enlargement. Treatment: a gingivectomy, or a full-thickness flap positioned apically. The fourth is excessive gingival display, the "gummy smile": the patient shows so much gingiva when smiling that they, or we, find it unesthetic. How much is too much varies a lot from country to country and culture to culture. Excessive gingival display: find the cause Its causes, which change what you can offer: short clinical crowns, because the anatomical crowns are naturally short or, more often, because the tissue still covers part of normal-length crowns (altered passive eruption); a vertical maxillary excess, where the teeth are normal in length and proportion but the maxilla itself is longer; or a short upper lip or a hypermobile upper lip, which moves more than normal from rest to full smile. It can be two or more of these together. The finding that points to each: abnormal tooth dimensions and proportions with gingival line asymmetries (altered passive eruption), an increased lower facial third (vertical maxillary excess), a lip under 20 mm long (a short lip), lip mobility over 8 mm (a hypermobile lip). Passive eruption and altered passive eruption Active eruption ends when the tooth meets its opponent in occlusion. Passive eruption follows: the mucogingival complex repositions apically around the crown until it settles at the cervical level, near the CEJ (Alpiste-Illueca). In altered passive eruption (some call it delayed passive eruption) that last step doesn't happen: the tissue still covers a good part of the crown, so the clinical crown is shorter than the anatomical crown. Coslet's classification reads it on two axes. The type is the band of gingiva. Type 1: a wider band, with the MGJ apical to the alveolar crest, always. Type 2: a normal band, with the MGJ usually at the level of the CEJ. The subcategory is the bone. A: the crest is in its normal range, 1.5 to 2 mm from the CEJ (the slide: more than 1 mm). B: the crest is within about 1 mm of the CEJ, or at it. All four combinations exist, and Types 1A and 1B are the most frequently encountered. His examples showed why the subcategory matters. In a Type 2B patient, with a normal band of attached gingiva and short clinical crowns, the full-thickness flap showed anatomical crowns far longer than what had been exposed, with the crest right at the CEJ on the central incisors. In a Type 1 patient (a wide band), the centrals were B, with the crest at the CEJ, and the laterals were A, with about 1.5 to 2 mm, so once the flap was raised bone came off the centrals but not the laterals. Teeth in one smile can need different treatment. Crown lengthening: the pretreatment evaluation Crown lengthening works on the difference between the clinical crown, what shows above the gingiva, and the anatomical crown, the enamel down to the CEJ. First the usual periodontal exam, because the patient has to be healthy: probing depth, plaque, bleeding on probing, attachment loss and the width of keratinized gingiva (measured from the MGJ to the gingival margin). Then the radiographs: the level of the alveolar crest, root length and form, and no active disease such as caries or a periapical lesion (the slides also list the apical extent of any fracture or caries, and pulpal involvement; Abou-Arraj and Souccar, 2013). Roots already shortened, by resorption or as a complication of orthodontics, limit how far a tooth can be lengthened. To find where the bone sits relative to the CEJ, numb the patient and sound to bone, probing through the attachment; a CBCT would also show it, but isn't typically taken for this kind of crown lengthening. The esthetic evaluation The patient is there for the smile, so an esthetic analysis follows, easiest from good extraoral and intraoral photos. Facial symmetry: right against left, with the interpupillary line, and the facial midline against the dental midline. Facial thirds: hairline to eyebrows (upper), eyebrows to subnasale (middle), subnasale to menton (lower). Compare the lower third with the middle third: ideally they're equal, and an increased lower facial third means the maxillary height is in excess (vertical maxillary excess). Still extraorally: the smile line (lip line). A low line shows no gingiva at full smile; a medium line shows up to 2 to 3 mm of gingiva, the ideal; a high line shows more. The incisal line, joining the incisal edges of the canines and incisors, should be consonant with the lower lip; everyone shows more of the lower teeth with age. Patients who don't like their gummy smile train themselves not to show it, so their posed smile hides gingiva that their unposed smile shows: draw out the real smile in conversation. Then the upper lip: its length at rest is 20-22 mm in women and 22-24 mm in men, and under 20 mm is a short upper lip; it normally moves 6-8 mm from rest to full smile, and more than 8 mm is a hypermobile upper lip. Intraorally, the teeth and gingiva, mainly to see whether there is altered passive eruption, which can be treated. Gingival line: the canines' margins level with the central incisors' (up to 1 mm more apical is accepted), and the lateral incisors about 1 mm coronal to both. The gingival zenith, the height of contour, sits slightly distal to the midline of each tooth, the canine included; from the front the canine's looks centered only because the canine sits at the corner of the arch. A periodontal probe checks the margins against each other. Tooth proportions: the golden proportion, which the slides show in nature, art and architecture. Seen from the front, if the lateral incisor is 1 wide, the central is about 1.6 and the visible canine about 0.6 (the slides: 1.618 : 1 : 0.618, a 9 mm central with a 5.56 mm lateral and 3.44 mm of canine). A central incisor's width should be about 75-80% of its length: a 10 mm long central should be at most about 8 mm wide, and 70-75% is acceptable, but not a square tooth; 50% is a mandibular incisor's shape. Abnormal proportions with gingival line asymmetries mean short clinical crowns, usually from altered passive eruption. (A worn dentition also gives short clinical crowns, from attrition, not altered passive eruption.) Treating excessive gingival display By cause. Altered passive eruption: crown lengthening, by gingivectomy or an apically positioned flap, with or without osseous surgery, plus restorative therapy when the patient's esthetic needs call for it (old restorations, veneers). Vertical maxillary excess: lengthening the teeth can't solve it, except a very minimal excess, because you can only expose crown, not root; it needs orthognathic surgery (a Le Fort, for example) with orthodontics, and periodontics may fine-tune the gingiva at the end. Hypermobile upper lip: Botox, which has to be repeated about every six months, or lip repositioning surgery, which ties the lip down closer to the MGJ but relapses in close to 50%; combined with Botox it does better. Short upper lip: no good options; dermal fillers can sometimes mask some of the display. Luckily it isn't the most common cause. With several causes, combine treatments. Crown lengthening by type The periodontal options are a gingivectomy, an apically positioned flap and osseous surgery, and the type decides which. A gingivectomy works only in Type 1A: there is a lot of gingiva to trim, and the bone is where it should be, so there is room for the supracrestal tissue attachment (the biologic width: connective tissue attachment and junctional epithelium) and the new margin stays where you put it. In Type 1B you could trim the extra gingiva, but with the bone at or near the CEJ there is no room for that attachment, so the tissue grows back almost to where it was: a gingivectomy there is only a short-term fix. Instead, make submarginal incisions, raise a full-thickness flap and do osseous surgery (ostectomy and osteoplasty) to recreate the same crest-to-CEJ distance at a more apical level. In Type 2 you can't afford to trim tissue, since the band is only of normal width: always leave no less than 2, ideally 3 mm of keratinized gingiva. So raise a full-thickness flap and position it apically, shifting the whole band without cutting any away: without osseous surgery in 2A, where the bone is where we like it, and with osseous surgery in 2B. In a periodontally healthy patient, osseous surgery that leaves a physiologic, positive architecture and no defects doesn't cause disease. Patient 1 A healthy 28-year-old woman with generalized fluorosis who disliked the color of her teeth. She declined orthodontics and wanted veneers, and was referred for an esthetic evaluation because of her inconsistent margins. Her facial thirds were equal, so no vertical maxillary excess; her midline was slightly off; her smile line was high, showing more than 3 mm of gingiva; her lower incisal line wasn't ideal, which is a restorative fix. Intraorally, #8 and #9 had flat heights of contour, and the laterals (#7 and #10) sat about 1 mm apical to the centrals instead of 1 mm coronal, with #6 and #11 asymmetric too. The centrals were square; the right lateral, #7, about 8 mm long and 6 mm wide, had near-ideal proportions. So #7 became the reference tooth: lengthening it would have meant moving everything else further apically. Ideally #6 would match #11, but that much lengthening would have exposed root, so the plan compromised on #6. Prosthodontics made a wax-up and a mock-up, and a guide made from the wax-up (today it can be a CBCT-planned, 3D-printed one) set the new margins. The surgeon and the restorative dentist have to agree on whether the incisal edges will be lengthened too. The surgery went one tooth at a time, starting with a central incisor, then matching the other to it, then the canines (more at #6 than at #11) and #10; #7, the reference, got only a sulcular incision. Up to there it looks like a gingivectomy, but he had sounded to bone and found the crest at or very close to the CEJ, so he raised a full-thickness flap (to the first molars, for access to the bone) and removed bone: the same amount of bone as soft tissue, 2 mm of bone for 2 mm of gingiva, to keep the relationship the soft and hard tissue had, shifted apically, so the result stays stable. An end-cutting bur marks the maximum height of the ostectomy; then the bone is blended like a crown margin, with osteoplasty between the roots, for a physiologic, positive architecture. The flaps were sutured back at the incisions. Sutures came out at 1 week; provisional veneers went on at 3 weeks, no sooner, with no subgingival preps while it heals; the definitive restorations waited six months, long enough for the tissues, the attachment and the bone remodeling to settle, which is why esthetic crown lengthening cases wait six months. Her final veneers are shown at 18 months. Abnormal color: the mucogingival tattoo The main reason for a metal tattoo in the gingiva is amalgam. When a root canal failed, apical surgery (an apicoectomy) cut off the root tip and retrofilled the canal with amalgam, which is no longer done, and the amalgam can leak into the tissue. His patient had had apicoectomies on four incisors, later lost them and had a six-unit bridge from canine to canine, with the stain over it. The fix is to remove the stained tissue and graft the area with tissue that has no discoloration. The recipient site is prepared split thickness ("partial thickness" on the exam means the same thing), and a free gingival graft cut to a template of the preparation is sutured in. Here the FGG isn't for root coverage or for keratinized gingiva; it replaces the discolored tissue. An FGG leaves a distinct border with the tissue around it, so after three months of healing it was blended in with a laser (a blade or a bur also works).
